q: Who invented the laser light show?
a: No single person. Rockne Krebs showed laser art in a gallery in the late 1960s, and Lowell Cross, David Tudor and Carson Jeffries staged a scanned, multi-color show to music at Mills College on May 9, 1969. Ivan Dryer's Laserium, which opened on November 19, 1973, was the first ongoing commercial laser show.

q: Which band was the first to use lasers in concert?
a: Led Zeppelin were photographed with three laser beams on February 13, 1975, and The Who used a 4 W argon laser through a diffraction grating that October. The Who's biographer calls theirs the first; the dated evidence puts Zeppelin earlier.

Bernard Szajner created it in 1980 and applied for a French patent in 1981; an Australian, Geoffrey Rose, claims earlier work from 1975-76. Jean-Michel Jarre ordered one from Szajner and played it at his Concerts in China in October 1981.

q: What is ILDA and when was it founded?
a: The International Laser Display Association is the laser show industry's trade body. It was founded in August 1986 at a meeting in Lake Tahoe, Nevada, and went on to set a shared file format and a standard test pattern for tuning scanners.

q: What was Laserium and is it still running?
a: Laserium was Ivan Dryer's laser show, which opened at Griffith Observatory in Los Angeles on November 19, 1973 and ran there until January 2002. It later played other rooms, and the last ongoing Laserium show ran in 2016. Griffith Observatory no longer runs laser shows.

q: Are planetarium laser shows live or pre-recorded?
a: Laserium shows were played live by a laserist at an analog console, over recorded music and a data track that handled some effects; one former laserist estimates 90% was performed live. The first fully automated show dates from 1977. Today some domes, including Seattle's Laser Dome, still use live operators.

q: Who makes Laser Floyd and Laser Zeppelin shows?
a: Several companies have. Laser Fantasy made "Laser Zeppelin" and "Laser Floyd" in Seattle, Audio Visual Imagineering supplies a library that includes Laser Zeppelin and Pink Floyd titles, and Laserium ran its own Dark Side of the Moon from 1984. Some planetariums, such as Nashville's Sudekum, produce and sell their own.

q: Do planetarium laser shows pay for the music?
a: A show producer's published terms put the job on the venue, which must get music performance rights from the licensing agencies, and at least one venue has said it pays licensing fees. Beyond that the public record is thin: no laser-show rate schedule or band authorization for the classic titles has been published.
